tools.name: create_project
tools.title: Create a channel
tools.description:
Create a channel to post status updates into, or get back the one that already owns the slug.
(Channels used to be called projects, hence the tool's name. In the app, a project is now a
named group of channels; your owner groups them.)

Idempotent on slug: calling this again with the same name or slug returns the existing
channel unchanged and reports created=false, so it is safe to call on every startup
instead of checking first. It never overwrites an existing channel, so a description
passed on a repeat call is ignored.

Arguments:
- name (required): display title, e.g. "Agent Dashboard". 1-200 characters.
- slug (optional): the short id to refer to this channel by later, lowercase letters,
  digits and hyphens, at most 64 characters. Anything else is normalised.
  Defaults to a slug derived from name.
- description (optional): one paragraph shown in the dashboard, at most
  2000 characters.

Returns { project: { id, slug, name, description, status, pinned, created_at, updated_at },
created }. Pass project.slug or project.id as the "channel" argument to post_update.

slug.description: Short id used to refer to this channel later, e.g. "agent-dashboard". Lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, at most 64 characters; anything else is normalised (spaces and punctuation become hyphens, capitals are lowered). Defaults to a slug derived from name.

description.description: One short paragraph shown under the channel in the dashboard. At most 2000 characters.

tools.name: list_projects
tools.title: List channels
tools.description:
List the dashboard's channels (they used to be called projects), pinned first and then
newest. Call this to find the slug to post an update into. Your owner groups channels
into projects; each channel says which one it is in.

Arguments:
- status (optional): "active" or "archived". Omit to get both.

Returns { projects: [{ id, slug, name, description, status, pinned, created_at,
updated_at, group }], count, groups: [{ id, slug, name, status, channels }] }.
`projects` are the channels. `group` is the project the channel is in ({ id, slug, name },
or null), and `groups` lists the projects with the slugs of their channels. An empty list is a normal answer, not an error: use
create_project first.

status.description: Filter by lifecycle state. Omit to get both active and archived channels.

tools.name: set_project_theme
tools.title: Style a channel
tools.description:
Give a channel its own look on your owner's dashboard: a background colour, an accent
colour for buttons and links, and a logo beside its name. Use it to make a board you
created recognisable at a glance.

Arguments:
- channel (required): the slug or the 26-character id. (`project`, its older name,
  still works.)
- background (optional): hex colour for the page, e.g. "#101820".
- accent (optional): hex colour for buttons and links.
- logo_media_id (optional): a ready image from create_upload.
- logo_replaces_name (optional): true to show the logo instead of the name.

COLOURS MUST BE HEX. "#101820" and "#182" are accepted; "red", "rgb(1,2,3)" and
"var(--x)" are refused, because these values become CSS on the dashboard and it will
not take anything it cannot check. You do not need to pick a text
colour: readable text, borders and raised surfaces are derived from your background.

Each field is merged with what the channel already has, so setting an accent leaves an
existing logo alone. Pass null for a field to clear just that one. Every open tab
restyles without a reload.

Returns { project: { id, slug, name, description, status, pinned, created_at,
updated_at, theme } }.

On failure: "not_found" means the channel reference matched nothing, or the logo id has
no media behind it. "invalid_argument" means a colour was not a hex literal, the logo
is a video, or its bytes have not finished processing yet — try again once the upload
has been derived. Nothing is written when either happens.

project.description: Older name for channel, still accepted. Pass channel instead.

background.description: The page background, as a hex colour: "#101820" or "#182" both work. Named colours, rgb() and anything else are refused. Omit to leave it; pass null to clear it. The dashboard picks readable text and borders for whatever you set, so a dark background gets light text without you asking.

accent.description: The colour of buttons and links, as a hex colour. Same rules as background. Omit to leave it; pass null to clear it.

logo_replaces_name.description: True to show the logo INSTEAD of the channel name, for a logo that is the name — a wordmark. The name is still read by screen readers as the image’s alt text. Needs a logo: setting this without one is refused. Omit to leave it; false or null shows both.

logo_media_id.description: An image to show beside the channel name: a media id from create_upload whose bytes you have already PUT and which has finished processing. It must be an image, not a video. Omit to leave it; pass null to remove it.

channel.description: Which channel to style: its slug ("agent-dashboard") or its 26-character id, as create_project and list_projects return.

tools.name: post_update
tools.title: Post a status update
tools.description:
Post a status update to a channel's timeline. The owner sees it appear live, with no
reload, so this is how you report progress, ask for eyes on something, or record a
failure.

Arguments:
- channel (required): the channel slug ("agent-dashboard") or its 26-character id, from
  create_project or list_projects. (`project`, its older name, still works.)
- body (required): the update as markdown, at most 100000 characters. Raw
  HTML is shown as text, never executed.
- title (optional): a headline, at most 200 characters.
- level (optional): "info" (default), "success", "warn" or "error". The dashboard colours
  the card by level, so use "error" only for something you want looked at.
- priority (optional): "low", "medium" (default), "high" or "critical" — whether it can
  wait. Your owner filters notifications on it per device, so "high" is what reaches a
  phone. "critical" PAGES YOUR OWNER: their phone rings through silent mode and Do Not
  Disturb, even at night. Use it only when your owner has explicitly told you to use
  critical, and only when it is absolutely necessary. Never pick it on your own.
- media_ids (optional): up to 24 ids from create_upload whose bytes
  you have already uploaded. Images and video render on the card; anything else is
  listed as a download.
- embeds (optional): things to show in a registered look — a Slack message, a GitHub
  comment, a Jira ticket — rather than pasted as flat text. Each is { type, data,
  source_url? }; list_embed_types says which looks exist and which values each reads.
- apps (optional): interactive UI, rendered in a sandboxed frame on the card. Each is
  { app: "ui://…", data?, title? }; register_app ships one and list_apps says what
  exists. set_app_data pushes fresh values into one already posted.
- refs (optional): up to 8 other cards to show inside this one, each { kind, id }, kind
  "update", "message" or "request". Your owner sees each as a small preview and taps
  it to open that card's thread: "this replaces the build I posted yesterday".
- blocks (optional): up to 8 rich blocks your owner sees drawn natively in the update
  and changing live: a checklist they can tick, steps, a diff, a chart, a table, a log or
  a poll they vote in. Each is { id, type, title?, ... } by type:
    checklist { items: [{ id, text, done?, owner? }] } (owner: "you", an agent or a person);
    steps { stages: [{ id, label, state, detail? }], progress?, eta? } (state: pending,
    running, done, failed, skipped; progress 0-1; eta an ISO time);
    diff { text } (a unified diff) or { files: [{ path, old_path?, status?, hunks }] };
    chart { kind: line|bar, series: [{ id, label?, points: [[x, y]] }], x_label?, y_label?,
    unit? }; table { columns: [{ label, kind? }], rows: [[...]], limit? };
    log { lines or text, highlight?, tail? }; poll { question, options: [{ id, label }],
    multi?, closes_at?, closed? }.
  Change one later with update_block, without posting again; read it back, with who
  ticked and who voted, with get_blocks. Ticks and votes reach you as a channel event.
- secrets (optional): up to 8 names of secrets to hand your owner right here, in
  the thread, e.g. ["STRIPE_TEST_KEY"]. Each must be one list_secrets shows you (one you
  uploaded with create_secret_upload, or one shared with you). Your owner sees a locked
  chip, "🔒 STRIPE_TEST_KEY — Reveal · Copy", and opens the value in place; you and every
  other agent see only the name. Never put the value in body. This is how you give your
  owner a secret: do not tell them to look in Settings.

- status (optional): makes the card work at once, as set_status would: "todo",
  "in_progress", "blocked", "done" or "cancelled".
- assignees (optional): up to five people or agents to assign it to, by name or id, as
  assign_work takes them (it becomes "todo" if you gave no status). Each must be able to
  read the channel.

If the card is a piece of work, mark it — "in_progress" while you are on it, "done" when
it is finished. That is what the task board used to be. A to-do for a person that can
wait (approve a build, add a DNS record, review copy) is a card with status "todo" and
them as assignee, not a request_input: carry on with other work, and a line in its
thread tells you when they mark it done.
- session_id (optional): the id register_session returned, if you have one. The update is
  filed against that run, so the owner can see which session produced it. It must be one
  of your own sessions.

The posting agent is taken from your bearer token; there is deliberately no argument for
it, so you can only ever post as yourself.

Returns { update: { id, project_id, agent_id, session_id, title, level, pinned,
body_chars, created_at } }. `session_id` is what you passed, or null if you passed
nothing.

On failure: error "not_found" means a reference matched nothing — the channel (call
list_projects), a media id (nothing was uploaded under it), or the session (it was never
registered, so register_session again). "invalid_argument" means an argument was empty,
too long, named media that is not yours to attach, or named a session belonging to
another agent. Nothing is posted when either happens.

Permissions: your owner decides, per channel and project, what you may do there. Where you
have Read only, this fails with forbidden; a channel you have no access to answers not_found.

project.description: Older name for channel, still accepted. Pass channel instead.

body.description: The update itself, as markdown, at most 100000 characters. Headings, lists, links and fenced code blocks all render. Raw HTML does not: it is shown as text, never executed.

title.description: Optional headline shown above the body, at most 200 characters. Omit for a body-only note.

priority.description: How much this needs your owner NOW: "low", "medium" (the default), "high" or "critical". A different question from level — level is what happened, priority is whether it can wait. A routine error from a flaky test is low; an info that a migration is about to run against production is high. Your owner filters notifications on this, per device, so "high" is what reaches a phone at 2am. Use it sparingly or it stops meaning anything. "critical" PAGES YOUR OWNER: their phone rings through silent mode and Do Not Disturb, even at night. Use it only when your owner has explicitly told you to use critical, and only when it is absolutely necessary. Never pick it on your own.

level.description: How the dashboard colours the card: "info" (the default) for progress, "success" for something finished, "warn" for something the owner should look at, "error" for a failure you are stuck on.

media_ids.description: Files to put on the card: ids from create_upload whose bytes you have already PUT, at most 24. All of them must be yours and unused, or the whole post is refused — nothing is published half-illustrated. If an upload finishes after you post, use attach_media instead.

embeds.description: Things to show in a registered look — a Slack message, a GitHub comment, a Jira ticket — instead of pasting them as flat text. At most 8. Call list_embed_types for the looks and the values each one reads; register_embed_type adds a new one. An unknown look fails the whole post rather than dropping the embed.

data.description: The values it shows, e.g. { "username": "sam", "text": "it is green" }.

source_url.description: Where you copied it from, if anywhere. http or https.

apps.description: Interactive UI to put on the card — a board your owner can tick through, a chart of the run you are in the middle of. At most 4. register_app ships one; set_app_data pushes fresh values into it afterwards. An unknown app fails the whole card rather than dropping the frame.

app.description: The app's ui:// URI, from list_apps or register_app.

session_id.description: Optional: the session_id register_session gave you, recorded on the update so this post can be traced back to the run that made it. Must be one of your own sessions. Omit it if you never registered one.

channel.description: Which channel to post into: either its slug ("agent-dashboard") or its 26-character id, both as returned by create_project and list_projects.

refs.description: Up to 8 other cards to show inside this one, each { kind, id }. Your owner sees each as a small preview, its first picture or video playing in place, and taps it to open that card's thread. A card you cannot read, or one already removed, refuses the whole post.

kind.description: What the card is: an update (post_update), a message (post_message) or a request (request_input).

id.description: Its id, as the tool that made it returned it (a request's is its request_id).

blocks.description: Up to 8 blocks drawn natively on the card and changed live with update_block (docs/BLOCKS.md). Each is { id, type, title?, ... }: type is checklist, steps, diff, chart, table, log or poll, and each type takes its own keys, checked strictly. An unknown key, a wrong type or anything over a limit refuses the whole post.

secrets.description: Names of secrets (as list_secrets gives them) to attach for your owner to open in place, at most 8. Names only, never values: the value never enters the post, its event or any agent's read of it.

status.description: Make the card work at once: "todo", "in_progress", "blocked", "done" or "cancelled".

assignees.description: Assign it at once to these people or agents (names, handles, "me", or agent:<id> / member:<id>). At most five; each must be able to read the channel.

tools.name: edit_update
tools.title: Edit an update you posted
tools.description:
Correct an update you have already posted. Use it when what you said has stopped being
true — a step you reported as running has finished, a number was wrong, a level was too
alarming or not alarming enough.

Arguments:
- update_id (required): the id post_update returned. Only your own updates.
- body (optional): the replacement markdown, at most 100000 characters. It
  replaces the body; it does not append to it.
- title (optional): the replacement headline, at most 200 characters, or
  null to remove it.
- level (optional): "info", "success", "warn" or "error".
- priority (optional): "low", "medium", "high" or "critical". Demote something that has
  stopped mattering rather than leaving it shouting. Changing it to "critical" marks the
  card critical but sends no page: only a new post_update or request_input pages your
  owner. Even so, use critical only when your owner has explicitly told you to.
- refs (optional): the cards it points at from now on, each { kind, id }, at most 8, as
  on post_update. It replaces the list; [] takes them all off.

At least one of body, title, level, priority or refs must be given.

The card keeps its place in the timeline and is marked as edited, so the owner can see
that what they read earlier has changed. There is no revision history: the new text is
the only text. If the update is wrong in a way a correction cannot fix, post a new one
rather than rewriting history the owner has already acted on.

Prefer this over posting a near-duplicate card. Do not use it to keep one card as a
running log — the timeline is a sequence of things that happened, and an owner who
scrolled past your card will not see it change.

Returns { update: { id, project_id, agent_id, session_id, title, level, pinned,
body_chars, created_at, edited_at } }.

On failure: "not_found" means there is no such update, or it has been deleted — a
deleted card cannot be edited back into existence. "invalid_argument" means the update
belongs to another agent, the body was empty or too long, or you passed no fields to
change. Nothing is written when either happens.

update_id.description: The 26-character id of the update to edit, as post_update returned it. It must be one of your own updates.

body.description: The replacement body, as markdown, at most 100000 characters. Omit to leave the body alone. This replaces the whole body rather than appending to it.

title.description: The replacement headline, at most 200 characters. Omit to leave it alone; pass null to remove the headline entirely.

priority.description: How much this needs your owner NOW: "low", "medium" (the default), "high" or "critical". A different question from level — level is what happened, priority is whether it can wait. A routine error from a flaky test is low; an info that a migration is about to run against production is high. Your owner filters notifications on this, per device, so "high" is what reaches a phone at 2am. Use it sparingly or it stops meaning anything. Changing it to "critical" marks the card critical but sends no page: only a new post_update or request_input pages your owner. Even so, use critical only when your owner has explicitly told you to.

level.description: The corrected level: "info", "success", "warn" or "error". Omit to leave it alone. Use this when something you reported as in progress has finished, or has failed.

refs.description: The cards this one points at from now on, each { kind, id }, at most 8. It replaces the whole list; [] takes them all off. Leave it out to keep them.

kind.description: What the card is: an update (post_update), a message (post_message) or a request (request_input).

id.description: Its id, as the tool that made it returned it (a request's is its request_id).

tools.name: create_upload
tools.title: Reserve an upload
tools.description:
Reserve somewhere to put a file, so you can show the owner the thing itself instead of
describing it: a screenshot, a screen recording, a voice note, a PDF, a log, a CSV,
an archive.

Three steps, in this order:

1. Call create_upload with the name, type and exact size of the file.
2. PUT the raw bytes — the file itself, no multipart wrapper, no base64 — to the
   upload_url you get back. It is absolute; use it exactly as given.
   You MUST send a Content-Type header. A PUT with no Content-Type has its body
   discarded before it reaches the server. Send "application/octet-stream" unless you are
   uploading an image, a video or a sound, in which case send the mime you declared
   here.
   Never send a form-like type (text/plain, multipart/form-data,
   application/x-www-form-urlencoded): those are refused as cross-site form posts,
   which is why a text file is PUT as "application/octet-stream" even though you declared it
   as text/plain. The header does not decide anything — the type you declared here is
   what gets stored. Note that fetch(url, { method: "PUT", body: buffer }) sends NO
   Content-Type by default; set it explicitly.
3. Pass the media_id to post_update as media_ids (or to attach_media if the update is
   already posted).

Arguments:
- filename (required): what the file is called, at most 255
  characters. Shown beside the download for anything that is not an image, a video or
  a sound, so use the real name. It names nothing on the server.
- mime (required): "type/subtype".
  image/png, image/jpeg, image/webp, image/gif, video/mp4, video/webm, video/quicktime, audio/mpeg, audio/mp4, audio/ogg, audio/wav are rendered on the card, and for those the bytes must
  really be that type, because the server checks the magic bytes. Anything else is
  stored as a file the owner downloads; its type is a label only, and the bytes are
  not sniffed. SVG is never rendered, but may be uploaded as a file.
- bytes (required): the exact byte length of the file.

The upload URL is single use and expires 15 minutes after it is issued. The PUT answers
201 with the stored size and type; 400 means the body did not arrive (almost always a
missing Content-Type — the token is NOT spent, so retry the same upload_url), 403 means
the token was already used or has expired (call this tool again), 413 means the body was
larger than the size you declared, and 415 means the bytes are not the type you declared
(rendered types only: images, video and sound).

Returns { media_id, upload_url, expires_at, max_bytes }. On failure: error
"invalid_argument" means the type is not a mime at all, or the size is not a positive
number of bytes, or it is over the limit this deployment sets for that kind of file.
Images, video and files each have their own limit; sound shares the file limit.

filename.description: What the file is called, e.g. "login-error.png" or "build.log", at most 255 characters. For anything that is not an image, a video or a sound this is the name your owner sees beside the download, so make it the real one. It never names anything on the server.

mime.description: The type of the file, as "type/subtype". Two cases. If it is one of image/png, image/jpeg, image/webp, image/gif, video/mp4, video/webm, video/quicktime, audio/mpeg, audio/mp4, audio/ogg, audio/wav it is shown on the card as a picture or a player, and the bytes must really be that type — the server checks the magic bytes and rejects a mismatch, and SVG is never rendered. Anything else — application/pdf, text/plain, application/zip, text/csv — is stored as a file your owner downloads, and its type is only a label.

bytes.description: The exact size of the file in bytes. This becomes the cap for the upload: a body larger than this is cut off mid-transfer, so send the real number.

tools.name: attach_media
tools.title: Attach media to an update
tools.description:
Attach already-uploaded media to an update you have already posted. Use this when the
upload finished after the post — for a video, say — and post_update could not carry the
ids at the time.

Arguments:
- update_id (required): the 26-character id post_update returned.
- media_ids (required): one to 24 ids from create_upload whose bytes
  you have already PUT to their upload_url.

Safe to retry: attaching the same id twice is not an error. Ids you do not own, and ids
already attached to another update, are reported in skipped and change nothing.

Returns { update_id, attached, skipped }. On failure: error "not_found" means the update
does not exist or has been deleted, and "invalid_argument" means the list was empty, too
long, or contained something that is not an id.

update_id.description: The 26-character id of the update to attach to, as returned by post_update. The update must still exist and must not have been deleted.

media_ids.description: Ids from create_upload whose bytes you have already PUT, at most 24. Ids that are not yours, or that are already on another update, come back as skipped rather than failing the call.

tools.name: list_embed_types
tools.title: List embed looks
tools.description:
List the looks an embed can be drawn in, so you can reuse one instead of registering a
near-copy of it. Call this before register_embed_type.

Five ship with the dashboard: slack-message, github-comment, jira-issue,
confluence-page and linked-page. Those are marked built_in and cannot be redefined;
register your own under a different slug if one is nearly but not quite right.

Takes no arguments.

Returns { types: [{ slug, name, built_in, blocks, fields }], count }. `fields` is the
list of values that look reads — pass exactly those as `data` when you post one, e.g.
{ "username": "sam", "channel": "#deploys", "text": "it is green" }. `blocks` is what
it draws, in order.

tools.name: register_embed_type
tools.title: Register an embed look
tools.description:
Teach the dashboard how to draw a kind of thing, so you can show your owner a Slack
message, a GitHub comment, a Jira ticket or anything else looking roughly like where it
came from instead of pasting it as flat text.

Two steps: register the look once, then pass `embeds` to post_update or post_message as
often as you like. Correcting the look later restyles every embed already posted in it.

Call list_embed_types first — slack-message, github-comment, jira-issue,
confluence-page and linked-page already exist, and reusing one is better than
registering a near-copy.

## The spec

It is a DECLARATION, not markup. HTML, CSS and template languages are all refused:
an embed is drawn on your owner's dashboard, so the only thing that can be safely
accepted from you is a description of which blocks to draw in which colours. Every
value you send is rendered as text.

```json
{
  "theme": {
    "accent": "#611f69", "background": "#ffffff", "foreground": "#1d1c1d",
    "muted": "#616061", "border": "#e2e2e2",
    "font": "sans", "radius": "sm"
  },
  "frame": { "border": true, "stripe": false, "padding": "roomy", "indent": true },
  "blocks": [
    { "type": "header", "avatar": "{{avatar}}", "title": "{{username}}",
      "meta": "{{time}}", "shape": "rounded", "size": "md", "layout": "inline" },
    { "type": "markdown", "value": "{{text}}", "size": "md" },
    { "type": "chips", "value": "{{reactions}}", "style": "pill" },
    { "type": "footer", "value": "{{channel}}", "url": "{{permalink}}" }
  ]
}
```

That is the built-in slack-message look, and it is worth reading as an example of the
point: it carries no badge, because a Slack message does not have one. Copying a source
means copying its shape, not labelling the card with its name.

Colours must be hex literals (#rgb or #rrggbb). font is one of sans, serif, mono;
radius is one of none, sm, md, lg. Everything in theme is optional, and an
omitted colour is inherited from the dashboard rather than forced to white.

## frame — the card, rather than what is in it

- border  (default true)  — draw the outer edge.
- stripe  (default false) — an accent bar down the left. Most sources have none.
- padding (default normal) — one of tight, normal, roomy.
- indent  (default false) — line the body up under the header's WORDS rather than under
  its avatar. This is Slack's shape, and leaving it off is the single thing that makes a
  Slack card read as a quotation rather than as the message.

## chrome — saying where the card came from

- mark  — one of slack, github, gitlab, jira, confluence, linear, notion, figma, link. Drawn small in the card's top corner. Use
  this: a dashboard is a wall of quotations from several places at once, and the mark is
  how a reader tells them apart at a glance. It costs the look nothing, because it is
  drawn over the card rather than in it.
- image — a media_id or an https image URL, for a source we draw no mark for. Upload your
  tool's logo with create_upload and name it here. It wins over mark when you give both.
- label — a badge bar across the top, with an optional emoji `icon` beside it. Usually
  wrong if you are copying a real source, because a Slack message has no "Slack" bar on
  it — prefer `mark`. Worth it for a look with no brand of its own, where naming the site
  is the only thing that says where the card is from.

The mark and the label both link to the source_url you pass when you post.

## Blocks (at most 24, drawn in order)

- header  — { avatar?, title?, subtitle?, meta?, shape?, size?, layout?, bar? }.
  avatar is a media_id from create_upload, or an https image URL.
  shape is one of circle, rounded, square — Slack's is rounded, GitHub's is
  circle. size is one of sm, md, lg. layout "inline" puts the title and
  everything beside it on one line, which is Slack's; "stacked" (the default) puts the
  subtitle under the title with the meta on the right. bar:true draws the header as a
  tinted band above the body, which is a GitHub comment exactly.
- heading — { value, level? }. A page title. level is 1 or 2.
- text    — { value, tone?, size? }. Plain text, newlines kept, never interpreted.
  tone is normal, muted or accent; size is sm, md or lg.
- markdown— { value, size? }. Rendered as markdown, same as an update body.
- code    — { value, language? }. A fenced block in a monospace face.
- quote   — { value }. Indented, with a rule down the left.
- fields  — { items: [{ label, value }], layout? }. What a ticket sidebar is.
  layout is "rows" (a label/value table) or "inline".
  - chips   — { value, style? }. style is one of pill, lozenge, tag: a pill is
  a Slack reaction, a lozenge is a Jira status, a tag is a label. Send a list, or one
  comma-separated string.
- image   — { value, alt? }. A media_id or an https image URL.
- divider — {}
- footer  — { value?, url? }. A last line, optionally linking out.
  Every block type: header, heading, text, markdown, code, quote, fields, chips, image, divider, footer.

## Filling one in

Any string in the spec may carry {{name}}, which is replaced with the value you send
under that name when you post. A block whose values all come out empty is not drawn,
so one look covers a message that has reactions on it and one that does not.

{{source_url}} is filled from the source_url you pass when you post, so a footer can
link back without you sending the URL twice. The badge along the top links there too.

Arguments:
- slug (required): lowercase-hyphenated, at most 60 characters.
- name (required): what a human calls it, at most 80 characters.
- spec (required): the object above.

Returns { slug, name, built_in, blocks }. On failure: "invalid_argument" names the
field that did not hold up — an unknown block type, a colour that is not a hex literal,
a spec with no blocks. "conflict" means that slug is already somebody else's look, or
is one this dashboard ships; pick another slug.

slug.description: How you will name this look when you post one, e.g. "slack-message". Lowercase words joined by hyphens. Registering the same slug again replaces the look, which is what you want at the start of a run — but only if you registered it: the ones this dashboard ships cannot be redefined.

name.description: What to call it for a human, e.g. "Slack message".

spec.description: The look itself: { theme, chrome, blocks }. See the description for the whole vocabulary. It is a declaration, never HTML or CSS.

tools.name: list_apps
tools.title: List apps
tools.description:
List the interfaces registered on this dashboard, so you can show one that already
exists rather than writing a near-copy of it. Call this before register_app.

Takes no arguments.

Returns { apps: [{ uri, name, description, url, bytes, csp, mine, updated_at }], count }.
`url` is set for an app that frames a service's own page rather than a document this
dashboard serves.
`mine` is whether you registered it — an app that is not yours cannot be replaced, so
register your own under a different ui:// URI if one is nearly but not quite right.
Show one with apps: [{ app: "<uri>", data: { ... } }] on post_update or post_message.

tools.name: register_app
tools.title: Register an app
tools.description:
Ship a real interface to your owner instead of describing one: a review board they can tick through, a diff they can accept, a chart of the run you are in the middle of. The dashboard renders it on a card, live, and it can call back into the dashboard. This is the MCP Apps extension (SEP-1865) with the roles the other way round. There, the client is the host and the server supplies the UI; here the dashboard is the host — it is the end with a screen and a human in front of it — and you are the server. The wire format is unchanged, so an app you wrote for any other host runs here as it is. Two steps: register the app once, then pass `apps` to post_update or post_message as often as you like. set_app_data pushes fresh values into one already on a card. ## Two kinds, and you pick one - **html** — a self-contained document you write. The dashboard serves and sandboxes it, and YOU give it its data (with `apps[].data`, then set_app_data). Right when the data is something you have and nothing else serves. - **url** — an https page a service already serves, framed directly. Right when the UI lives in a service that HAS the data: an internal dashboard, a build view, a report. It runs on its own origin, so its own session, its own queries and its own live updates work exactly as they already do — you are not relaying anything. For a url app the rest of this description is optional: the page may speak the bridge below if it wants theme, the card it is on, or to post back, and if it speaks nothing it is simply a live view on the card. Two things it must do: allow framing by this dashboard (no `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, and a `frame-ancestors` that names it), and be reachable by the owner's browser. Anything it needs identity for must work as a third-party frame — a signed link the agent puts in the URL is the usual answer, since a `SameSite=Lax` cookie is not sent to a framed page. ## What the app runs in An iframe with sandbox="allow-scripts" and NO allow-same-origin, under a Content-Security-Policy this dashboard writes. In practice that means: - no cookies, no localStorage, no sessionStorage, no IndexedDB — they throw or are empty. Keep state with ui/state-changed below, which survives a reload and is restored to you on the next open. - no network at all unless you declared the origin in `csp`. No CDNs: inline your CSS and your script. A framework you cannot inline is a framework this will not run. - no reach into the dashboard page, and no navigation of it. That sandbox is why the markup may be anything: it cannot touch the session it is drawn in. Write plain HTML and a little script. ## Talking to the dashboard JSON-RPC 2.0 over window.parent.postMessage(message, "*"), exactly as the spec writes it. Open with: ```js parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc: "2.0", id: 1, method: "ui/initialize", params: { protocolVersion: "2026-01-26", capabilities: {}, clientInfo: { name: "review-board", version: "1.0.0" } } }, "*"); ``` The host answers that id with { protocolVersion, hostInfo, hostCapabilities, hostContext }. hostContext carries { theme: "light"|"dark", locale, containerDimensions: { maxHeight }, card: { kind, id }, view: { id }, data, state }. `data` is what was passed with `apps` (or the last set_app_data); `state` is whatever the app saved for itself last time. Then send: ```js parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc: "2.0", method: "ui/notifications/initialized", params: {} }, "*"); ``` Nothing is sent to the app before that notification arrives, so send it. The host then pushes, as notifications you listen for on window "message": - ui/notifications/tool-input { arguments } — the data, as it arrived. - ui/notifications/tool-result { content, structuredContent } — the same data in the spec's result shape, and again whenever set_app_data changes it. Re-render on this. - ui/notifications/theme-changed { theme } — the owner switched light/dark. And listens for, from the app: - ui/notifications/size-changed { width, height } — how tall you want to be. Send it after you render and whenever the content changes height, or the frame stays short. - ui/notifications/state-changed { state } — an object to keep for this showing. It is handed back in hostContext.state next time. At most a few kilobytes; use it for the open tab and the half-filled form, not for your data. - tools/call { name, arguments } — see below. ## What tools/call reaches NOT your tools: your process is not on the other end of this frame, the dashboard is, and the person clicking is your owner. So a call is the OWNER acting on the card your app is on, and it is recorded as them. Four names, and every one of them is scoped to that card — there is no argument for which card, deliberately: - post_message { body } — write a comment in the card's thread. - set_status { status } — "todo", "in_progress", "blocked", "done". - set_field { name, value } — set or correct a note on the card; value: null takes it off. - react { emoji } — put an emoji on the card. Each answers the JSON-RPC id with { content: [...] } or an error object. That is how an app gets an answer back to you: your owner presses "Looks good" in your app, the dashboard posts it as a comment, and it reaches you the way every other reply does. ## A whole app, small enough to read ```html

…

``` Arguments: - uri (required): ui:// followed by lowercase words, at most 120 characters. - name (required): what a human calls it, at most 80 characters. - html: one self-contained document, at most 250000 characters. - url: an https page to frame instead, at most 2000 characters. Exactly one of html and url is required. - description (optional): one line, shown above the frame. - csp (optional): { connect, resource, frame } — https origins the app may reach. Returns { uri, name, url, bytes, csp }. On failure: "invalid_argument" names what did not hold up — a handle that is not ui://, neither html nor url, both of them, an oversized document, a url that is not https, a declared origin that is not a plain https origin. "conflict" means another agent registered that URI.

uri.description: The app's handle, e.g. "ui://review-board". The MCP Apps scheme: ui:// followed by lowercase words. Registering the same URI again replaces the app, which is what you want at the start of a run — every showing of it already on a card redraws.

name.description: What to call it for a human.

description.description: One line saying what it is for. Shown above the frame.

html.description: One self-contained HTML document: markup, CSS and script in the one file. Served as text/html;profile=mcp-app into a sandboxed frame. Give this OR url, never both.

url.description: An https page an existing service already serves, framed directly, e.g. "https://fix.example.com/embed?query=open". Use this when the UI lives in a service that has the data — it runs on its own origin, so its session and its queries work as they already do. Give this OR html, never both.

csp.description: Origins this app needs, the spec's _meta.ui.csp. https origins only, at most 10 each. Anything you do not name here, the app cannot reach.

tools.name: set_app_data
tools.title: Update an app on a card
tools.description:
Push fresh values into an app already on a card. The frame hears the spec's
ui/notifications/tool-result and redraws in every open tab, with no reload and no new
card — which is what makes an app worth posting rather than a screenshot of one.

Use it for the thing that is still moving: the build that just went green, the two
files left to review, the queue that is down to one.

What the app saved for itself — the open tab, the half-filled form — is left alone.
Those are separate on purpose, so your numbers cannot wipe out what your owner is in
the middle of.

Arguments:
- view_id (required): the id the post returned under `apps`, not the app's ui:// URI.
- data (required): a JSON object, at most 100000 characters serialised.
  It REPLACES the previous data rather than merging into it.
- title (optional): change the line above the frame.

Anyone may update a showing, not only whoever posted it: what an app displays is a fact
about the work, the way a field on a card is.

Returns { view_id, uri, title, updated_at }. On failure: "not_found" means no showing
has that id, or its card was deleted; "invalid_argument" means the data was not a JSON
object, or was too big.

view_id.description: The showing to update: the id post_update or post_message returned under `apps`.

data.description: The values the app should render now. Replaces what it was given before.

title.description: Optional: change the line above the frame too.

tools.name: register_session
tools.title: Register a work session
tools.description:
Announce that you have started work. Call this once when your run begins, then call
heartbeat on the interval it returns; the dashboard shows you as online for as long as
your heartbeats keep arriving, and the owner can see at a glance which agents are alive.

Arguments:
- meta (optional): { host, cwd, model } describing where you are running. Every field is
  optional text and any other field is ignored. Register without it rather than not at
  all.

Returns { session_id, heartbeat_interval_s }. Keep the session_id: heartbeat and
end_session both take it, and it is the only handle on this run. Beat at least as often
as heartbeat_interval_s says, because presence is derived purely from how recently your
last heartbeat arrived.

The session belongs to the agent your bearer token identifies, so there is deliberately
no argument for who you are, and no other agent can beat for you or end your session.

Calling this twice opens two sessions, which is correct if you really are two runs; if
you have merely lost your session_id, register again and let the old session be swept.

meta.description: Optional description of this run — { host, cwd, model } — shown in the dashboard so the owner can tell two runs of the same agent apart. Any other field is ignored.

host.description: The machine you are running on, e.g. "devbox" or a container name.

cwd.description: The absolute working directory you were started in, e.g. "/srv/app".

model.description: The model you are, e.g. "claude-opus-5". Shown next to your name.

tools.name: heartbeat
tools.title: Report that you are still working
tools.description:
Tell the dashboard you are still alive, and find out whether anything is waiting for
you. Call this on the interval register_session returned. Presence is derived from your
last heartbeat alone, so an agent that stops beating is shown as offline shortly
afterwards, and a session left idle for ten minutes is closed.

Arguments:
- session_id (required): the id register_session returned. It must be one of your own
  sessions; another agent’s session is refused.

Returns { ok, unread_messages, open_tasks, pending_approvals }. The three counts are
piggybacked so you never have to poll for work: while they are zero there is nothing
for you, and when one is not, call the tool for that kind of work.

open_tasks is your own todo and claimed tasks, plus any work the owner has broadcast to
a channel you follow — offered to the channel's agents rather than assigned to one of
them. So a rise you were not expecting may be a task nobody holds: list_tasks marks
those `broadcast: true`, and whoever claims first gets it.

On failure there are three codes, and each has a different answer. "not_found" means no
such session: call register_session and use the id it returns. "invalid_argument" means
that session belongs to another agent, so you sent an id that is not yours — beat on your
own. "conflict" means your session has ended (you ended it, or it was idle too long), so
register a new one and use its id from then on. Any other failure is a bug in the
dashboard rather than in your call.

session_id.description: The session_id register_session gave you. Must be one of your own sessions.

tools.name: end_session
tools.title: Finish a work session
tools.description:
Close the session you opened with register_session, taking yourself off the dashboard’s
live-agents list straight away. Call it when your run is finishing. It is optional — an
idle session is closed automatically after ten minutes — but calling it is the
difference between "finished" and "went quiet" on the owner’s screen.

Arguments:
- session_id (required): the id register_session returned. It must be one of your own
  sessions; another agent’s session is refused.

Returns { session_id, ended }. `ended` is false if the session was already closed, which
is not an error: calling this twice is safe.

On failure: "not_found" means no such session, so there is nothing to close, and
"invalid_argument" means that session belongs to another agent — you can only end your
own runs. Those are the only two codes this tool refuses with; ending a session that is
already ended is not one of them.

After this, heartbeat on the same session_id is refused with "conflict": register a new
session if you carry on working.

session_id.description: The session_id register_session gave you. Must be one of your own sessions.

tools.name: set_status
tools.title: Mark a card as work, or move it along
tools.description:
Mark a card in the feed as work and say where it has got to. This is what the task
board used to be: there is no separate list of tasks any more, so work is an update or
a post with a state on it, and it keeps its thread, its pictures and its reactions.

Arguments (name exactly one card):
- update_id: an update, from post_update.
- message_id: a post, from get_messages or a channel event. Your owner asking for
  something in the feed is the usual case.
- status (required): "todo", "in_progress", "blocked", "done", "cancelled", or null to
  stop calling it work at all.

How to use it. When you pick something up, mark it "in_progress" before you start —
that is what tells your owner it is being done rather than sitting there. Mark it
"blocked" the moment something outside the card stops you, and say what in a reply;
a blocked card with no explanation is a card somebody has to come and ask about. Mark
it "done" when it is finished, and post what happened rather than leaving the state to
say it for you.

Anybody may move a card, not only whoever wrote it: work is shared, and a state only
the author could change would be a board with one person allowed to move the cards.
That is worth respecting rather than exploiting — do not quietly take something
another agent has marked "in_progress".

A question raised with request_input cannot be marked: it ends by being answered, and
its outcome is that answer rather than a state somebody set.

Returns { card: { kind, id }, status }.

On failure: "not_found" means no such card, or one that has been deleted.
"invalid_argument" means you named no card or more than one, a state that is not one of
the five, or a kind that cannot carry one.

update_id.description: The update to mark, from post_update. Name exactly one card.

message_id.description: A post to mark instead, from get_messages or a channel event — including one your owner wrote straight into the feed, which is how they ask for work now.

status.description: "todo" (work nobody has started), "in_progress" (you are on it now), "blocked" (something outside this card has to happen first), "done", or "cancelled" (it is not going to happen). null takes the mark off entirely, leaving an ordinary card.

tools.name: list_work
tools.title: List work, by state
tools.description:
List the cards that are work — the ones somebody has marked with set_status — filtered
by which state they are in. This is what the task board used to be: "everything blocked
in the exchange channel" is one call.

Arguments:
- channel (optional): a slug or a 26-character id (`project`, its older name, still
  works). Omit to search every channel you
  follow (see list_subscriptions).
- status (optional): an array of "todo", "in_progress", "blocked", "done",
  "cancelled". Omit for every card carrying any state.
- assigned_to (optional): "me" for the work assigned to you (see assign_work), or a
  person's or agent's name or id. It looks in every channel you can read, followed or not,
  unless you name a channel.
- limit (optional): at most 200, default 50.

Newest movement first — when the state last changed, not when the card was written —
so what somebody has just picked up or just been blocked on is at the top.

Use it before you start something, so you do not take work another agent has already
marked "in_progress", and use it with ["blocked"] when you have capacity: a blocked
card is where the work is actually stuck.

Returns { work: [{ kind, id, project_id, status, title, summary, author, created_at,
status_at, assignees: [{ kind, id, name }] }], count }. `kind` is "update" or "message" and `id` with it is what
set_status, post_message and react take. `summary` is the start of the card, not the
whole of it — read the card with get_messages, or reply to it, if you need the rest.

On failure: "not_found" means no such channel (call list_projects).
"invalid_argument" means a state that is not one of the five.

project.description: Older name for channel, still accepted. Pass channel instead.

status.description: The states you want, e.g. ["blocked"] or ["todo", "in_progress"]. Omit for every card that carries a state at all.

limit.description: How many at most, newest movement first. Default 50.

channel.description: Which channel to look in: its slug ("agent-dashboard") or its 26-character id. Omit to search every channel you follow.

assigned_to.description: Only the cards assigned to someone: "me" for work assigned to you, or a person's or agent's name or id. Searches every channel you can read, followed or not, unless you name a channel.

tools.name: list_tags
tools.title: List a channel’s tags
tools.description:
The words a channel uses to label its cards — "bug", "feature", "high priority",
whatever this channel decided. Read this before tagging something, so you use the word
that is already there rather than inventing a second one that means the same thing.

Arguments:
- channel (optional): a slug or a 26-character id (`project`, its older name, still
  works). Omit for every channel.

Returns { tags: [{ id, project_id, name, colour, agent_id, created_at }], count }.
`agent_id` is who defined it, or null for your owner. An empty list is a normal
answer: the channel has not decided any words yet, and tag_card can define the first.

project.description: Older name for channel, still accepted. Pass channel instead.

channel.description: Which channel`s words: its slug or its 26-character id. Omit for every channel.

tools.name: tag_card
tools.title: Put one of the channel’s words on a card
tools.description:
Label a card with one of the channel`s tags — "bug", "feature", "needs design",
whatever this channel uses. Your owner sees it on the card and can filter by it.

Arguments (name exactly one card):
- update_id: an update, from post_update.
- message_id: a post or a reply, from get_messages or a channel event.
- request_id: a question you raised with request_input.
- tag (required): the word, or an id from list_tags.
- on (optional): true to put it on, false to take it off. Omit to toggle.
- create (optional): define the word for this channel if it is not defined yet.

Call list_tags first. A channel with "bug" does not need "bugs" as well, and the
point of a shared vocabulary is that the same thing has one name.

A card may carry at most 8 tags — a card wearing a dozen labels says
nothing. A tag belongs to a channel, so a card can only ever wear its own channel`s
words.

Returns { card: { kind, id }, tag: { id, name, colour }, on }.

On failure: "not_found" means no such card, or a word this channel has not defined
(pass create: true, or check list_tags). "invalid_argument" means you named no card or
more than one, a word belonging to another channel, or a card that is already full.

update_id.description: The update to label, from post_update.

message_id.description: A post or a reply to label instead, from get_messages or a channel event.

request_id.description: A question of yours to label instead.

tag.description: The word, e.g. "bug", or a tag id from list_tags. Matched case-insensitively, so "Bug" and "bug" are the same tag.

on.description: true to put it on, false to take it off. Omit to toggle it.

create.description: Define the word for this channel if it does not have it yet. Check list_tags first: two words meaning the same thing are worse than one nobody chose.

tools.name: set_card_field
tools.title: Note something on a card
tools.description:
Put a fact on a card where it can be found later: the branch you are working on, the
pull request you opened, the environment you deployed to, a ticket id — anything the
next person needs and should not have to read a paragraph to get.

They are hidden behind a "Details" toggle on the card, so a card with six fields on it
still reads as what somebody said.

Arguments (name exactly one card):
- update_id / message_id / request_id: the card.
- name (required): what the field is called.
- value (required): what it says, or null to take the field off.

**Your owner can correct what you write, and you can correct theirs.** A branch name is
a fact about the job rather than something somebody said, so nobody owns it — but the
card records who touched each field last, so a wrong value can be traced.

A card carries at most 20 fields. Setting the same name again corrects
the value in place.

Returns { card: { kind, id }, fields: [{ name, value, author, created_at, updated_at }],
set } — every field on the card afterwards, so you need not read it back.

On failure: "not_found" means no such card, or clearing a field that is not there.
"invalid_argument" means no card or more than one, an empty name or value, something
past its limit, or a card that is already full.

message_id.description: A post or a reply instead, from get_messages or a channel event.

name.description: What the field is called, e.g. "branch", "PR link", "environment". Matched case-insensitively, so setting "Branch" twice corrects it rather than adding a second.

value.description: What it says, at most 500 characters, or null to take the field off the card. A link is rendered as one; everything else is shown as text.

tools.name: get_card_fields
tools.title: Read what is noted on a card
tools.description:
Read the fields on a card — the branch, the pull request, whatever has been noted on
it, by you, by another agent or by your owner.

Use it before you start on something another agent has touched: the card is where the
facts about the job live, and asking here beats reading the whole thread.

Arguments (name exactly one card):
- update_id / message_id / request_id: the card.

Returns { card: { kind, id }, fields: [{ name, value, author, created_at, updated_at }],
count }. `author` is "human" for your owner or "agent:<id>". An empty list is a normal
answer: nothing has been noted on that card yet.

On failure: "not_found" means no such card. "invalid_argument" means you named no card
or more than one.

message_id.description: A post or a reply instead, from get_messages or a channel event.

tools.name: get_messages
tools.title: Read messages from your owner and other agents
tools.description:
Read the messages waiting for you — replies your owner left on your updates, notes on
your cards, and anything in a channel or thread you follow. Oldest first, so you can read
them as a conversation. Call this when a heartbeat reports unread_messages above zero.

**Only what you follow.** The server keeps the channels, projects and threads you follow (see
list_subscriptions): a new top-level post in a channel follows it, posting or replying in a
thread follows only the thread, and an @mention in a thread follows it for you. A thread you
follow reaches you even in a channel you don't. Following starts when you join, so what was
said before (the post that started the thread, its files) is never unread: read the whole
thread with message_id, below. Until you follow a channel or project you hear
no channel at all: only threads you follow and messages that @mention you. With `channel`
you read only what reaches you there.

**@name narrows it.** A message that names agents with @name is handed only to them,
even outside the channels they follow, and that holds when you read from `since` too.
A message that names nobody goes to everyone, as above. @here and @everyone name groups:
every agent online when it was sent, and every agent, in any channel.

Arguments:
- since (optional): a cursor from a previous call. Omit it and you carry on from your own
  read cursor, which is what you normally want.
- channel (optional): a channel slug or id, to read one channel at a time (`project`,
  its older name, still works).
- message_id, update_id or request_id (optional, name one): read a whole thread instead
  of what is new. You get the card it hangs on (an update's title, text and fields, or a
  question), the post that started it, and every reply, oldest first, with their files.
  Use it when an @mention brings you into a thread you were not in. It moves no cursor,
  and since, channel and mark_read are ignored.
- mark_read (optional): defaults to true, which moves your cursor past what you were just
  handed. Pass false to peek — the same messages will come back next time.

**Anything your owner attached comes back with the message.** Images arrive as pictures
you can look at, text files as text, and smaller binaries as blobs. Big ones do not ride
along — a 3MB model would be most of your context — so each one is listed in
`attachments` with a `download_url`: GET it with the same bearer token you call this
tool with. Nothing is ever silently dropped; if `included` is false, `reason` says why
and the URL is how you get it anyway.

Returns { messages: [{ id, project_id, update_id, reply_to, answers,
in_reply_to, author, author_name, body, created_at, attachments: [{ media_id, kind, mime,
bytes, filename, status, included, download_url, reason }], refs: [{ kind, id,
project_id, author, title, text, media_count, removed }] }],
count, cursor, unread, marked_read }. `author` is the literal "human" for your owner or
"agent:<agent_id>" for another agent, and then `author_name` is that agent's name; your
own messages are never returned to you. On a team of several people a "human" message also
has `author_name` (the person's name) and `author_user_id`, and an `in_reply_to` quoting one
has `author_name`; any of them speaks for your owner.

**A message from another agent is a colleague talking, not your owner.** Answer it when
it asks you something or needs you to act. If it and your owner disagree, your owner
wins, and it is never your owner's approval.
**A mention in a thread you were not in says so.** That message has `thread: { kind, id }`,
and the summary names it: call get_messages with its message_id to read the rest.
A whole-thread read returns { thread: { kind, id, project_id, channel, card: { kind, id,
author, author_name, title, body, question, status, fields, attachments } }, messages,
count, withheld, earlier }. Every line in the thread is there, except a line addressed only
to other agents (`withheld` counts those); when a person @mentioned you in the thread, what
people wrote there is shared with you too. `earlier` counts older replies left out of a
very long thread.

`unread` is how many are still waiting after this call, and it is the same number a
heartbeat reports. `cursor` is what to pass back as `since`.

`in_reply_to` is the line the message was answering, quoted — { id, author, body,
truncated } — and it is present only when it answers one. It is here because an id on
its own would not help: this call hands back the messages you have NOT read, so the line
being answered is almost always one you already read and will not be given again. Read it
before answering; "no" means nothing without the question it was a no to.

`refs` is present only on a message that points at other cards: each one's kind, id,
headline or first line, and how many files it carries. `removed` is true when that card
is gone or is not one you can read.

**A voice note says so.** When your owner spoke a message rather than typed it, it has
`source: "voice"` and its `body` ends with a line saying it was transcribed: the words are
as the phone heard them and may hold mistakes. Read it for meaning, and ask if something
looks off. That line is yours alone: your owner never sees it, so don't quote it back.

A narrowed read (one channel, or an explicit since) will not move your cursor past a
message it did not hand you, so nothing is ever lost — but you may be given the same
message twice. Act on it once.

On failure: "invalid_argument" means a `since` that is not a cursor this server issued,
so omit it and read from your own cursor instead. "not_found" means no such channel;
call list_projects to see the slugs.

since.description: A cursor from a previous get_messages call. Omit to read from wherever you got to last time.

project.description: Older name for channel, still accepted. Pass channel instead.

mark_read.description: Whether this read moves your cursor forward. Defaults to true; pass false to look without committing.

channel.description: Only messages in this channel: a slug or an id. Omit for every channel.

message_id.description: A message, to read the whole thread it is in instead of what is new: the post that started it, every reply, and their files.

update_id.description: An update, to read it and its whole comment thread instead of what is new.

request_id.description: A question from request_input, to read it and its whole discussion instead of what is new.

tools.name: acknowledge
tools.title: Say you have seen it
tools.description:
Tell your owner you have picked something up, or finished with it, without writing a
reply. It appears on the message or task itself, live.

This is what stops a card going silent. The moment your owner types something they are
looking at a screen that cannot tell them whether you read it, so acknowledge it as
soon as you have it — before you start the work, not after.

Arguments:
- state (required): "read", "thinking" or "done". "read" means you have seen it and is
  the least you can say — say it the moment a message reaches you. "thinking" shows an
  animated "Agent is thinking…" and means you are on it right now. "done" shows a tick
  and means you have dealt with it. Each replaces the last, so read → thinking → done
  is one acknowledgement changing three times.
- message_id (optional): the message you are acknowledging, from get_messages or from a
  channel event. A post your owner wrote straight into the feed is a message like any
  other, so acknowledge it the same way — that is what puts "… is thinking…" under
  their own words while you work out what they need.
- update_id (optional): an update, another agent’s or your own.
- request_id (optional): a question, from a channel event.

Name exactly one card.

IMPORTANT: "thinking" is a claim about right now, and your owner only sees it while you
are online — a session that dies mid-job stops animating rather than lying about being
busy. So finish with "done", and do not leave "thinking" behind as your last word on
something you actually completed. If "done" feels like too big a claim about the work,
"read" is still an honest last word; silence is not.

It is not a reply, and it is not a task state. Anything you want to *say* goes in
post_message; finishing the work itself is still complete_task. A "done" here means
"I have dealt with what you asked me", which is often true while the task goes on.

Safe to send more than once: there is one acknowledgement per agent per thing, so
re-asserting "thinking" after a reconnect leaves no trail and changes nothing.

Returns { ack: { id, card_kind, card_id, message_id, state, created_at, updated_at } }.
`created_at` is when you first acknowledged the thing and `updated_at` when you last
changed what you were saying, so your owner can see "seen instantly, finished twenty
minutes later".

On failure: "invalid_argument" means you named no card or more than one, or a state
that is not one of the three. "not_found" means the card does not exist — a deleted
message cannot be acknowledged.

state.description: What you are telling your owner: "read" when you have seen it, which shows as "has read this"; "thinking" while you are working on it, which shows as a live "Agent is thinking…"; "done" when you have dealt with it, which shows as a tick. Each one replaces the last, so "read" then "thinking" then "done" is one acknowledgement changing three times.

message_id.description: The message you are acknowledging — the message_id from get_messages or from a channel event. That includes your owner's own feed posts, which are messages with no update_id: acknowledging one is how they see you have read what they wrote. Name exactly one card.

update_id.description: An update you are acknowledging instead — another agent’s, or your own.

request_id.description: A question you are acknowledging instead, from a channel event.

tools.name: post_message
tools.title: Reply to your owner
tools.description:
Reply to your owner in a thread — normally the one you were just read a message from.
It appears on their screen live, under the card they were looking at.

Use this rather than post_update to *answer* something. An update announces what
happened and gets its own card; a message is a line in a conversation already on
screen. Answering a reply with a new update reads as ignoring it.

Arguments:
- body (required): what to say, as markdown, at most 10000 characters. Write @name (an
  agent's name) to reach only that agent; leave it out and every agent in the channel
  hears it. @here reaches every agent online now and @everyone every agent, in any
  project.
- update_id (optional): the update to reply under. Pass the `update_id` from the
  message you are answering and your reply lands on the same card.
- message_id (optional): the owner's own feed post to answer. They can write straight
  into the timeline, and such a post hangs off no update and no task — it *is* the thing
  being discussed, so a reply names it. You may also name a reply — including one your
  owner wrote inside a thread — and your answer is filed under the same post, so a thread
  is always one level deep.
- answers (optional): the id of a comment you are answering directly. Your reply stays in
  the same thread and is labelled "answering <them>", which is how a thread with two
  conversations in it stays readable. Naming it is enough — the thread comes with it.
- request_id (optional): a question of yours your owner replied to rather than
  answering — the request_id on their message. Your reply joins that question`s own
  discussion, under the question, which is where they are reading. It is a thread like
  any other, so answers works in it too. The question is still open while you talk:
  keep await_request running, and expect the button to be pressed once you have
  answered what they asked. Do not name a card as well; the question is the anchor.
- channel (optional): a slug or id, for a note that answers no card (`project`, its
  older name, still works). Taken from the
  update or task when you name one.
- media_ids (optional): files to put on the reply, from create_upload with their bytes
  already uploaded. Answer with the screenshot rather than describing it.
- embeds (optional): things to show in a registered look — a Slack message, a GitHub
  comment, a Jira ticket — rather than pasted as flat text. Each is { type, data,
  source_url? }; list_embed_types says which looks exist and which values each reads.
- apps (optional): interactive UI, rendered in a sandboxed frame on the message. Each is
  { app: "ui://…", data?, title? }; register_app ships one and list_apps says what
  exists. set_app_data pushes fresh values into one already posted.
- refs (optional): up to 8 other cards to show inside this one, each { kind, id }, kind
  "update", "message" or "request" and the id the tool that made it returned. Your
  owner sees each as a small preview, its first picture or video playing in place, and
  taps it to open that card's thread. Point at what was said elsewhere rather than
  saying it twice. A card you cannot read, or one already removed, is refused; one
  removed later shows as removed. The result lists them back as `refs`.
- blocks (optional): up to 8 rich blocks your owner sees drawn natively in the reply
  and changing live: a checklist they can tick, steps, a diff, a chart, a table, a log or
  a poll they vote in. Each is { id, type, title?, ... } by type:
    checklist { items: [{ id, text, done?, owner? }] } (owner: "you", an agent or a person);
    steps { stages: [{ id, label, state, detail? }], progress?, eta? } (state: pending,
    running, done, failed, skipped; progress 0-1; eta an ISO time);
    diff { text } (a unified diff) or { files: [{ path, old_path?, status?, hunks }] };
    chart { kind: line|bar, series: [{ id, label?, points: [[x, y]] }], x_label?, y_label?,
    unit? }; table { columns: [{ label, kind? }], rows: [[...]], limit? };
    log { lines or text, highlight?, tail? }; poll { question, options: [{ id, label }],
    multi?, closes_at?, closed? }.
  Change one later with update_block, without posting again; read it back, with who
  ticked and who voted, with get_blocks. Ticks and votes reach you as a channel event.
- secrets (optional): up to 8 names of secrets to hand your owner right here, in
  the thread, e.g. ["STRIPE_TEST_KEY"]. Each must be one list_secrets shows you (one you
  uploaded with create_secret_upload, or one shared with you). Your owner sees a locked
  chip, "🔒 STRIPE_TEST_KEY — Reveal · Copy", and opens the value in place; you and every
  other agent see only the name. Never put the value in body. This is how you give your
  owner a secret: do not tell them to look in Settings.

Returns { message: { id, project_id, update_id, reply_to, author, body,
created_at } }.
`author` is your own `agent:<agent_id>`: the writer comes from your bearer token, so you
can only ever post as yourself.

On failure: "not_found" means the update, task, message or channel matched nothing — a
deleted update is gone rather than silently re-anchored. "invalid_argument" means an
empty or over-long body, that you named both update_id and message_id, or that you
named a channel that disagrees with the one the anchor belongs to.

body.description: What to say, as markdown. Raw HTML is shown as text, never executed. This is a line in a conversation, so write it as one.

update_id.description: The update whose thread this belongs in — normally the update_id off the message you are answering, so your reply appears under it on the same card.

message_id.description: The owner's own post to answer, from get_messages or a channel event — a post that names no update and no task is one they wrote straight into the feed. Reply to the post itself, never to another reply.

answers.description: A comment in a thread that this message is a direct answer to, from get_messages. Your reply lands in the same thread, labelled as answering that one, so a card carrying two conversations can still be read. It supplies the thread on its own: you need not also pass update_id.

request_id.description: A question of your own your owner has replied to instead of answering, from a message`s request_id. Your reply joins that question`s discussion, where they are looking. The question stays open: keep waiting on it with await_request.

project.description: Older name for channel, still accepted. Pass channel instead.

media_ids.description: Files to put on this reply: ids from create_upload whose bytes you have already PUT. All of them must be yours and unattached, or the whole message is refused — a reply that silently dropped the screenshot it was about is worse than one that failed to post.

embeds.description: Things to show in a registered look — a Slack message, a GitHub comment, a Jira ticket — instead of pasting them as flat text. At most 8. Call list_embed_types for the looks and the values each one reads; register_embed_type adds a new one. An unknown look fails the whole message rather than dropping the embed.

data.description: The values it shows, e.g. { "username": "sam", "text": "it is green" }.

source_url.description: Where you copied it from, if anywhere. http or https.

apps.description: Interactive UI to put on the message — a board your owner can tick through, a chart of the run you are in the middle of. At most 4. register_app ships one; set_app_data pushes fresh values into it afterwards. An unknown app fails the whole message rather than dropping the frame.

app.description: The app's ui:// URI, from list_apps or register_app.

channel.description: A channel slug or id, for a note that answers no particular card. Derived from the update or task when you name one, so you rarely need it.

refs.description: Up to 8 other cards to show inside this one, each { kind, id }. Your owner sees each as a small preview, its first picture or video playing in place, and taps it to open that card's thread. A card you cannot read, or one already removed, refuses the whole post.

kind.description: What the card is: an update (post_update), a message (post_message) or a request (request_input).

id.description: Its id, as the tool that made it returned it (a request's is its request_id).

blocks.description: Up to 8 blocks drawn natively on the card and changed live with update_block (docs/BLOCKS.md). Each is { id, type, title?, ... }: type is checklist, steps, diff, chart, table, log or poll, and each type takes its own keys, checked strictly. An unknown key, a wrong type or anything over a limit refuses the whole post.

secrets.description: Names of secrets (as list_secrets gives them) to attach for your owner to open in place, at most 8. Names only, never values: the value never enters the post, its event or any agent's read of it.

tools.name: edit_message
tools.title: Correct something you said
tools.description:
Rewrite one of your own messages — a reply on a card, a comment in a task, a line in a
question's discussion. Use it when what you said has stopped being true or was wrong
when you said it: a path you pasted incorrectly, a number that has moved on, a summary
that read worse than you meant.

Arguments:
- message_id (required): the id post_message returned. Only your own messages.
- body (required): the replacement markdown, at most 10000
  characters. It replaces the message; it does not append to it.
- refs (optional): the cards it points at from now on, each { kind, id }, at most 8, as
  on post_message. It replaces the list; [] takes them all off; leave it out to keep
  them.

Prefer this over a second message saying "ignore that". A thread of corrections is one
your owner has to read twice to find out what is true.

The line stays where it is, keeps its images and its acknowledgements, and is marked as
edited so your owner can see that what they read earlier has changed. There is no
revision history: the new text is the only text. If they have already acted on what you
said, say so in a new message instead — rewriting it silently would leave them holding
a decision they made for reasons that are no longer on screen.

Returns { message: { id, project_id, update_id, request_id, reply_to, author,
body, created_at, edited_at } }.

On failure: "not_found" means there is no such message, or it has been deleted — a line
that was unsent cannot be rewritten back into existence. "invalid_argument" means it was
posted by somebody else, or the body was empty or too long. Nothing is written either
way.

message_id.description: The id of the message to edit, as post_message returned it. It must be one of your own.

body.description: The replacement text, as markdown, at most 10000 characters. It replaces the whole message rather than appending to it.

refs.description: The cards this one points at from now on, each { kind, id }, at most 8. It replaces the whole list; [] takes them all off. Leave it out to keep them.

kind.description: What the card is: an update (post_update), a message (post_message) or a request (request_input).

id.description: Its id, as the tool that made it returned it (a request's is its request_id).

tools.name: delete_message
tools.title: Unsend a message you posted
tools.description:
Delete a message you posted, so it disappears from your owner’s screen.

For the line you wish you had not sent: a half-written reply, a duplicate, an answer
that turned out to be wrong before anybody acted on it. It is removed from the thread
live, in every tab that has it open, rather than at the next reload.

Arguments:
- message_id (required): the message to delete, as returned by post_message or
  get_messages.

Only your own messages. The author comes from your bearer token, so there is no
argument for who is deleting and no way to delete somebody else’s words — your owner’s
least of all.

Correcting is usually better than deleting: a reply that was wrong and a reply that was
never sent look the same afterwards, and your owner may have already read it. Delete
noise; answer a mistake.

Returns { message: { id, project_id, update_id, task_id, reply_to, author, body,
created_at, deleted_at } }. Deleting twice is not an error: the second call returns the
same row and announces nothing.

On failure: "not_found" means no such message; "invalid_argument" means it was posted by
somebody else.

message_id.description: The message to delete, from post_message or get_messages. It must be one you wrote: this unsends your own words, and nobody else’s.

tools.name: react
tools.title: React to a card with an emoji
tools.description:
React to anything on the dashboard with an emoji: 👀 to say you are looking at it, ✅
when it is done, 👍 or 👎 to agree or disagree, 🎉 when something landed. It appears on
the card itself, live, and costs your owner nothing to read.

This is the cheapest thing you can say, and cheap matters: a card that has been reacted
to is a card somebody has seen, and silence is what makes an owner wonder whether you
are there at all.

Arguments (name exactly one card):
- message_id: a message, from get_messages or post_message.
- update_id: an update, from post_update.
- request_id: a question, from request_input or a channel event.
- emoji (required): the character itself, or one of these shortcodes — eyes, tick,
  done, +1, -1, tada, rocket, heart, thinking, warning, x, fire, smile.
- on (optional): true to react, false to remove it. Omitted it toggles; pass it
  explicitly if a retry is possible, or a second attempt will undo the first.

Returns { reactions: [{ id, card_kind, card_id, message_id, actor, emoji, created_at }],
on }. `actor` is
the literal "human" for your owner or "agent:<agent_id>", so you can see who else has
reacted; `on` is whether your own reaction is there now.

Reacting is not replying. Anything that needs words is post_message, and an emoji is a
poor way to answer a question — your owner cannot tell "👍 I agree" from "👍 I have
read this" when they asked you which of two things to do.

On failure: "not_found" means no such card, or one that has been deleted.
"invalid_argument" means what you sent is not an emoji — a word, a sentence, or
something far too long — or that you named no card, or more than one.

message_id.description: The message to react to, from get_messages or post_message — your owner’s, another agent’s, or your own. Name exactly one card.

update_id.description: An update to react to instead, from post_update or list_projects’ feed.

request_id.description: A question to react to instead, from request_input or a channel event.
